findings.title: Credential-sync responses are returned in a shape incompatible with several refresh callers
findings.body: The sync branch returns the raw Fetch Response, whereas the original refresh functions return provider SDK/Axios results. Google Calendar reads `res.data`, and HubSpot, Zoho CRM, and Zoho Bigin all read fields through `.data`; a Fetch Response has neither parsed data nor those token fields. With syncing enabled, token refresh for these integrations therefore reads undefined values or throws instead of using the synchronized access token. The helper must normalize the sync response to the contract expected by each caller (or all callers must explicitly parse `response.json()`).

findings.title: The permissive sync schema strips the expiry field supplied by the credential service
findings.body: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is a Zod object and Zod objects strip unknown properties by default. The computed keys do not make it a catch-all schema, so a sync response such as `{ access_token, expiry_date }` is parsed down to just `access_token`; the function then injects a fake refresh token. Callers that require expiry information, notably Zoom's `newTokens.expires_in`, persist an invalid/NaN expiry and subsequently try to refresh again using the fake refresh token. Use `.passthrough()`/`z.record` as appropriate and preserve the documented expiry field, or normalize it explicitly for each provider.

findings.title: Google credential updates store Zod's SafeParse result instead of credential keys
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the complete `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), but this value is written directly to `Credential.key`. Google credential loading later parses `credential.key` as the Google token object, so after the first refresh the stored wrapper no longer has top-level `access_token`, `refresh_token`, or expiry fields and the integration becomes unusable. Persist `key.data` after checking success, not the SafeParse result.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sends the credential ID as the Cal.com user ID to the sync endpoint
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects its third argument to be the credential owner user ID and sends it as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, which is the database credential primary key. The self-hosted credential service will look up the wrong user (or no user), so Bigin refresh fails or can retrieve another user's token when numeric IDs happen to overlap. Pass `credential.userId` through this refresh path instead.

findings.title: Salesforce service references Prisma without importing it
findings.body: The newly added refresh logic calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file has no `@calcom/prisma` import. TypeScript compilation fails with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, blocking builds that include the app-store package.

findings.title: Concurrent credential webhooks can create duplicate credentials
findings.body: The endpoint implements an upsert as a `findFirst` followed by a separate create/update, but the lookup is not protected by a transaction or a unique `(userId, appId)` constraint. Two simultaneous webhook deliveries for a user without a credential can both observe no row and create separate credentials. Several integration paths use `findFirst`, so which synced credential is used becomes nondeterministic and stale credentials remain active. Use an enforced unique key with upsert, or serialize/retry this operation.
